fields.sections.0.h: The Life and Engineering Legacy of a Pioneer
fields.sections.1.h: The Leap to the Apollo Program
fields.sections.2.h: Innovation in Problem-Solving and Defensive Programming
fields.sections.3.h: The Apollo 11 1202 Error and Priority-Based Software
fields.sections.4.h: Establishing the Authenticity of Software Engineering
fields.sections.5.h: Public Recognition as a Hero and Cultural Legacy
fields.sections.6.h: Death in 2026 and Legacy in the Technology Industry
fields.sections.0.ko: Margaret Hamilton was born in Indiana in 1936, studied mathematics at the University of Michigan, and earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics from Earlham College. In 1959, she moved to Boston to follow her husband's law studies and began developing weather prediction software at MIT's Department of Meteorology, an experience that influenced subsequent research by Professor Edward Lorenz, famous for chaos theory. In 1961, while developing software for the SAGE Project, America's first air defense system at MIT's Lincoln Laboratory, she became interested in software reliability, a field that was largely unexplored territory at the time.
fields.sections.1.ko: In 1965, Hamilton learned through a newspaper advertisement that MIT's Instrumentation Laboratory was recruiting software developers for lunar landing software. She applied and was hired as the first programmer on the Apollo Project and the first female programmer within the project. Starting with software development for unmanned Apollo missions, she was promoted to lead the team developing on-board flight software for crewed missions, and by 1968 she led a team of over 400 members responsible for the lunar module and command module.
fields.sections.2.ko: Hamilton demonstrated exceptional leadership alongside sharp problem-solving abilities, capabilities that saved the Apollo Project from crisis multiple times. An incident known as the "Lauren Bug," in which her daughter Lauren executed a pre-launch program during a flight simulator run, led to the addition of software to prevent this program's execution during flight and served as an early example of defensive programming. Initially rejected on the grounds that highly trained astronauts would not make the same mistake, the error actually occurred during the Apollo 8 mission in 1968 when Jim Lovell made the identical mistake, validating Hamilton's proposal when it was integrated into the program.
fields.sections.3.ko: In July 1969, just before the Apollo 11 lunar landing, the lunar module's on-board computer detected a 1202 error, caused by computer overload due to a hardware switch malfunction. However, the priority-based software developed by Hamilton and her team was able to terminate unnecessary background tasks and concentrate processing power on mission-critical operations. When the Houston Flight Control Center trusted Hamilton's software and decided to continue the mission, humanity was able to set foot on the Moon for the first time.
fields.sections.4.ko: Hamilton devoted her life to establishing software engineering as an independent academic discipline. When she first used the term "software engineering," the industry treated it as a joke, but through her persistent advocacy and efforts, the software field came to receive equal respect as other engineering disciplines. She founded Higher Order Software in 1976, and a decade later established Hamilton Technologies to innovate the software development process based on error prevention and fault tolerance. The company's flagship product, the Universal Systems Language (USL), became a standard for complex software system design.
fields.sections.5.ko: Hamilton's achievements were recognized through the 2003 NASA Outstanding Space Law Award, the 2016 Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Barack Obama, the 2017 Computer History Museum Fellowship Award, the 2019 Unimaginable Achievement Award, and induction into the National Aviation Hall of Fame in 2022. In 2015, the entire Apollo software developed by her team was made publicly available on GitHub, and in 2017, a Hamilton minifigure was included in the LEGO Women of NASA series designed by MIT science communicator Maia Weinstock and distributed worldwide. In later years, a famous photograph of her standing next to her Apollo code printout taken at MIT's laboratory became widely shared online, making her a symbol of inspiration for women in science and technology.
fields.sections.6.ko: Margaret Hamilton passed away on September 30, 2026, at the age of 90. Working at MIT from 1959 through the mid-1970s and authoring over 130 academic papers, she was central to the process of establishing software engineering as an independent field. Professor Olivier de Weck, Apollo Project professor, evaluated her as a figure who laid the foundation for modern software engineering and as a precedent for establishing practices based on problem-solving and systems engineering. She is survived by her daughter Lauren Hamilton, son-in-law Richard Seleznick, two grandchildren, and four great-grandchildren, with a memorial service scheduled for spring 2026 in Cambridge.
